title: NovaDocs x Redwood Inference — Discovery (Embeddings + Rerank)
summary: NovaDocs walked through their RAG search stack (embeddings + vector DB + reranking) and current pain around cost per query and latency at peak. Redwood discussed hosted embeddings/rerank options, batching and caching levers (including request coalescing + query/result caching patterns), and how Redwood Optimize/Console can validate cost-per-query improvements. NovaDocs expressed interest in a public-facing architecture diagram and a performance/cost story if results are strong, but noted they need to avoid exposing customer names and internal infra specifics.
topics: Current NovaDocs search pipeline: embeddings + vector DB + reranker
Latency targets (p95) and peak traffic shape
Cost per query drivers: embedding calls + rerank calls + retries
What can be shared publicly (architecture diagram, anonymization)
questions: Can Redwood support separate models for embeddings and reranking with version pinning?
How does Redwood batching impact tail latency for rerank workloads?
What caching patterns are safe (query cache vs prefix/KV cache) for this use case?
How do you measure and publish cost-per-query improvements credibly?
action_items: Redwood (Simran): Send a proposed measurement plan for cost-per-query (baseline window, traffic sampling, what to log).
Redwood (Hannah): Share a short list of recommended embedding + rerank model candidates and expected unit costs to sanity-check fit.
NovaDocs (Maya): Provide an anonymized breakdown of current query volume, average docs per query to rerank, and current p50/p95 latency.
NovaDocs (Eli): Confirm whether NovaDocs prefers a hosted POC first or wants a Dedicated capacity discussion later.
next_steps: Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive next week focused on rerank throughput + batching and a caching plan (query/result cache).
NovaDocs to share a small set of representative queries + expected result sizes (topK) for benchmarking.
If the POC is greenlit, Redwood will spin up an eval endpoint and set up Console dashboards for latency/cost tracking.
Marketing follow-up (optional): outline what a public architecture diagram could look like and approval workflow.
transcript:
Meeting: NovaDocs x Redwood Inference — Discovery (Embeddings + Rerank)
Recorded: May 9, 2025 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 44 min

Attendees
- Hannah Schmitt (Redwood) — AE
- Simran Kaur (Redwood) — Solutions Architect
- Eli Park (NovaDocs) — CTO
- Maya Singh (NovaDocs) — ML Engineer
- Jonah Reyes (NovaDocs) — PM, Search


[Auto Summary]
NovaDocs is running an embeddings + vector DB retrieval pipeline followed by reranking. They are cost sensitive and seeing spend spikes tied to rerank calls and retries. They want to reduce cost per query without breaking relevance. They’re open to Redwood hosted endpoints and want guidance on batching/caching. They also mentioned they’d be interested in a public architecture diagram / customer story if the numbers are meaningful and the write-up can be anonymized.


[00:00:03] Hannah Schmitt: Cool, thanks everyone for making the time. I’m Hannah, I run a lot of the platform-ish evals on the commercial side. Simran is here too, she’ll go deep on the technical details. Before we dive in, does it make sense if we do quick intros and then we can map what you’re doing today?

[00:00:18] Eli Park: Yeah. I’m Eli, CTO at NovaDocs. We do, uh, document search for B2B SaaS teams, like internal knowledge bases. We’ve been shipping a RAG thing for… about a year.

[00:00:33] Maya Singh: Maya, ML engineer. I own most of the retrieval pipeline and the model evals.

[00:00:38] Jonah Reyes: Jonah, PM for search. I’m here to represent what product cares about, which is like “don’t break relevance” and “don’t double the bill.”

[00:00:47] Simran Kaur: Hi all, Simran. I’m solutions architect at Redwood. I help with POCs and performance measurements.

[00:00:55] Hannah Schmitt: Great. So, what prompted the conversation? Is it mostly cost, latency, or both?

[00:01:02] Eli Park: Both. Like, cost is the thing that keeps showing up in our weekly finance thread. But the proximate pain is p95 latency. We get tickets when search feels sluggish.

[00:01:15] Hannah Schmitt: Got it. Can you walk us through the request path today? Like query comes in, what happens.

[00:01:22] Maya Singh: Sure. A query hits our API. We generate an embedding. That’s currently OpenAI embeddings. Then we hit Pinecone for topK retrieval. Then we rerank. Rerank is Cohere right now.

[00:01:39] Maya Singh: And then we return top… usually 5, sometimes 10. We also do some snippet extraction, but that part is cheap.

[00:01:49] Simran Kaur: When you say rerank, are you sending like, query + N passages, right? What’s N on average?

[00:01:56] Maya Singh: We try to keep N around 30 but it varies. Some customers set it to 50. We cap at 60.

[00:02:04] Simran Kaur: Okay. That’s helpful.

[00:02:07] Hannah Schmitt: And traffic shape? Like QPS, bursts, or is it steady.

[00:02:12] Eli Park: It’s bursty. We’re multi-tenant. During business hours, it clusters. Maybe… average a few queries per second overall, but peak can be 10x. The worst is when a big customer does like a training or onboarding session and everyone searches at once.

[00:02:32] Jonah Reyes: Also, we have this “typeahead-ish” experience in one product surface. We throttle it but it’s still… there’s a lot of repeated queries.

[00:02:41] Hannah Schmitt: Oh that’s interesting. Repeated queries is like the classic caching win.

[00:02:46] Maya Singh: Yeah, except it’s not always exact repeat because users type “how do I reset…” and then “how do I reset password” and then “how do I reset password in Okta” you know.

[00:02:56] Simran Kaur: Right, so you get prefix overlap. You can still do caching strategies, just have to be careful with correctness and TTLs.

[00:03:05] Hannah Schmitt: Where do you feel the cost is mostly? Is it embeddings, rerank, both?

[00:03:10] Eli Park: Rerank. Embeddings are not free, but rerank cost is… it really spikes. And when Pinecone returns a bunch of candidates, it’s like we are paying per passage basically.

[00:03:25] Jonah Reyes: Plus we do retries. Like, timeouts occasionally. So we pay twice sometimes.

[00:03:31] Hannah Schmitt: Makes sense. And what’s the latency target? Like, what do you want p95 to be.

[00:03:36] Jonah Reyes: Product wants sub-one-second. Realistically, we’re okay if it’s like 1.2 seconds p95 end-to-end. But right now we see 2 seconds sometimes.

[00:03:49] Maya Singh: End-to-end includes vector DB and rerank. Rerank itself can be… like 400 to 800ms depending on payload.

[00:03:58] Simran Kaur: Payload meaning number of passages plus passage length.

[00:04:02] Maya Singh: Yep.

[00:04:05] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. So, for Redwood, the way customers tend to approach this: either you swap the embedding endpoint, swap the rerank endpoint, or both. Sometimes you keep your current vector DB, sometimes you change it, but that’s not required. We’re mostly in the “model inference” portion.

[00:04:23] Hannah Schmitt: You mentioned OpenAI + Cohere today. Are you open to open models, or do you prefer hosted proprietary.

[00:04:31] Eli Park: We’re open. But we care about quality. We did some tests with smaller embedding models and it tanked relevance.

[00:04:38] Maya Singh: We can evaluate. I’m not religious about provider. But we need stable versioning. We’ve been burned when a model changes under us.

[00:04:48] Simran Kaur: Version pinning is a common ask. Redwood supports pinning to a model version, plus staged rollouts. Also for the measurement side, Redwood Console can show cost and latency per route.

[00:05:01] Jonah Reyes: Is that like a dashboard? Or do we have to instrument everything ourselves?

[00:05:07] Simran Kaur: You’ll have request IDs and you can integrate tracing if you want, but out of the box you get token/cost latency breakdowns at the inference layer. For embeddings and rerank, it’s not “tokens” in the same sense but we still break down per request and throughput.

[00:05:22] Hannah Schmitt: And there’s an “Optimize” toolkit where we give suggestions like “batch these requests” or “set this cache TTL” based on observed traffic. It’s not magic, but it helps you get to a plan.

[00:05:35] Maya Singh: Can you talk about batching? Like, rerank seems hard to batch because it’s already a list of passages.

[00:05:43] Simran Kaur: Good question. There’s two notions of batching. One is inside a single rerank call you already have N passages. Another is multiple rerank requests arriving around the same time. If you have typeahead-ish traffic, you might be able to micro-batch across requests with a small max-wait like 5–20ms and still not hurt p95. But it depends on your SLO.

[00:06:07] Simran Kaur: The other lever is reducing candidate set size before rerank. Like better retrieval filtering. That’s not Redwood-specific, but we can help test whether a smaller topK preserves quality.

[00:06:19] Jonah Reyes: We’ve tried reducing topK and it hurts recall, then support complains.

[00:06:25] Maya Singh: It’s tenant-dependent. Some customers have messy docs.

[00:06:29] Hannah Schmitt: Right. We probably don’t want to assume topK goes down. So we focus on: can rerank be cheaper, can it be faster, and can we avoid reranking when it’s basically the same query.

[00:06:42] Eli Park: Yeah caching is appealing. We do some caching at the API layer for exact query strings for like 60 seconds. But it’s not huge.

[00:06:52] Simran Kaur: When you say caching, are you caching final results or intermediate? Like embeddings.

[00:06:58] Maya Singh: Final results for the exact query string. We don’t cache embeddings explicitly. OpenAI has their own—well, not caching, but it’s fast enough.

[00:07:07] Simran Kaur: There’s a pattern where you can cache the embedding vector for query prefixes in typeahead flows. But correctness is tricky. Another pattern is caching the rerank output keyed by (query, docIDs, doc versions). If docs don’t change too often, you can do a short TTL and get big hits.

[00:07:27] Jonah Reyes: Our docs do change, like edits. But not second-to-second.

[00:07:32] Eli Park: For most tenants it’s like weekly or daily. Some sync more often.

[00:07:37] Hannah Schmitt: That’s typically workable with a TTL plus invalidation on doc updates for big tenants.

[00:07:44] Maya Singh: Do you support caching inside Redwood? Or is it “bring your own Redis.”

[00:07:49] Simran Kaur: We do some platform-side caching like prefix/KV caching for generation-style models. For embeddings and rerank, the usual setup is you implement query/result caching in your app tier, because it depends on business logic. But we can recommend patterns and we can help you measure hit rates.

[00:08:09] Hannah Schmitt: Another angle is unit cost. If you’re using a rerank model that is expensive, sometimes there are alternatives that have similar relevance on your dataset but lower cost. We can run that eval with you.

[00:08:23] Maya Singh: Is that an offline eval? Like, we can give you labeled data?

[00:08:27] Simran Kaur: Ideally yes. Even implicit labels are fine—clickthrough, “user selected result” signals. If you don’t have labels, we can do A/B online with guardrails, but it’s more involved.

[00:08:42] Jonah Reyes: We have click signals, but they’re noisy.

[00:08:46] Hannah Schmitt: Noisy is still useful. We can also do “golden query sets” with your team.

[00:08:52] Eli Park: I’m trying to keep this scoped. Like, we don’t want a 3-month science project.

[00:08:58] Hannah Schmitt: Totally. On typical POC for this, we aim for 2–3 weeks: baseline measure, swap endpoint, measure again, and produce a simple “cost per query” before/after and latency before/after.

[00:09:14] Simran Kaur: And we document the measurement notes so it’s reproducible. Like time window, payload sizes, what’s included/excluded.

[00:09:24] Maya Singh: Okay. What do you need from us to do that.

[00:09:28] Simran Kaur: A few things: representative query distribution (typeahead vs full query), typical passage lengths, and average topK. Also whether you can replay traffic safely in a staging env.

[00:09:44] Eli Park: We can do traffic replay for a subset. We can’t send customer docs out of our environment though.

[00:09:52] Simran Kaur: Understood. For hosted API, the model sees the text you send, so if that’s a blocker, we might need to talk about VPC/private. But based on your note, I’m not sure you’re in that category.

[00:10:07] Eli Park: Not yet. We’re not in HIPAA or anything, but we do have enterprise customers that are picky. We can anonymize some content, maybe.

[00:10:16] Maya Singh: We can redact PII. But it’s the doc content itself that is the value.

[00:10:22] Hannah Schmitt: That’s fair. For a discovery, we don’t need to solve governance today. But it’s important. Redwood does have Dedicated and Private options; most SaaS folks start hosted, then if procurement forces it, we migrate to Dedicated. Private is usually regulated.

[00:10:39] Jonah Reyes: What’s the difference cost wise between hosted and dedicated.

[00:10:43] Hannah Schmitt: Dedicated is a commit for capacity—predictable throughput. Hosted is usage-based. For your stage, hosted is typically easiest to start. If you want predictable p95 at peak and you’re getting throttled today, Dedicated can help.

[00:10:59] Maya Singh: We do get rate limits from providers. It’s not constant but it’s annoying.

[00:11:03] Eli Park: Especially during launches.

[00:11:06] Simran Kaur: For rerank, the payload size also triggers rate limiting with some providers. Redwood can be more flexible because we control the runtime. But we need to see the shapes.

[00:11:18] Hannah Schmitt: Can I ask what you’ve tried so far on cost reduction? Any knobs you already pulled.

[00:11:23] Maya Singh: We tried lowering topK. We tried truncating passages more aggressively. That helped cost but hurt relevance on longer docs.

[00:11:34] Maya Singh: We also tried skipping rerank for some “simple” queries, but we don’t have a good classifier.

[00:11:41] Jonah Reyes: The skipping logic created weird edge cases where results looked random.

[00:11:47] Simran Kaur: That’s common. One approach is a two-stage rerank: cheap rerank to narrow, then expensive rerank only on top 10. Or use a cheaper cross-encoder for most and a better one for “hard” queries.

[00:12:05] Maya Singh: That’s interesting. But again, more complexity.

[00:12:09] Hannah Schmitt: We can keep it simple by focusing on swapping provider first and measuring. If we get a win, we can decide whether to add advanced routing later.

[00:12:20] Eli Park: Okay. We’re open to a quick POC. What kind of “win” do customers usually see.

[00:12:27] Hannah Schmitt: Depends on baseline, but for cost-per-query on rerank heavy workloads, we’ve seen 20–40% reductions when we switch models and tune batching. For latency, often a few hundred milliseconds off p95. I don’t want to promise a number without seeing your data.

[00:12:46] Jonah Reyes: We’d want at least like 25% cost reduction or p95 under 1.2 sec, something like that.

[00:12:55] Simran Kaur: We should set acceptance criteria like that. Also define the measurement window. Like “weekday traffic 9–5 PT” or a replay dataset.

[00:13:07] Maya Singh: Yeah, and we need to make sure we don’t accidentally compare apples to oranges.

[00:13:12] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[00:13:14] Hannah Schmitt: Switching gears slightly—Jonah, you mentioned product cares about not breaking relevance. How do you evaluate relevance today.

[00:13:23] Jonah Reyes: Mostly user feedback plus some internal smoke tests. We have like 50 queries we run manually.

[00:13:32] Maya Singh: I have a small eval harness. It’s not fancy. We can add more.

[00:13:37] Simran Kaur: That’s enough for a POC. We can start with your 50 plus maybe we add 50 more from logs.

[00:13:46] Eli Park: What about embeddings. Would you recommend changing embeddings too or only rerank.

[00:13:52] Simran Kaur: Usually the biggest lever is rerank. Embeddings change can have broader impact and might require re-indexing, which is heavy. So I’d start with rerank.

[00:14:04] Maya Singh: Thank you, yes, re-indexing is not fun.

[00:14:08] Hannah Schmitt: We can do rerank-only POC: keep OpenAI embeddings, keep Pinecone, just replace Cohere rerank. That keeps scope contained.

[00:14:20] Jonah Reyes: That sounds good.

[00:14:22] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. On content marketing—this might be early, but you brought up interest in a public architecture diagram. Can you say more? Some customers want to share “high level” without numbers.

[00:14:35] Eli Park: Yeah, we do content marketing. We have a blog. People like architecture posts. If Redwood helps us cut cost/latency, we’d be willing to do a joint post. But we can’t share customer names, and we can’t share like “here’s our exact AWS account setup.”

[00:14:52] Jonah Reyes: Also we would want to control the narrative. Like, no “NovaDocs was broken” vibe.

[00:14:57] Hannah Schmitt: Totally. The usual is: problem statement, constraints, solution architecture, and measured outcomes. We can anonymize specifics and focus on “multi-tenant SaaS doc search” and show a generic diagram.

[00:15:13] Simran Kaur: And for the diagram, we can do something like: API → embeddings → vector DB → rerank → results. You can label it at a conceptual level.

[00:15:24] Maya Singh: That seems doable. We’d need legal review internally, but conceptually yes.

[00:15:31] Hannah Schmitt: Great. No pressure now. We can revisit once we have data.

[00:15:36] (crosstalk)

[00:15:37] Eli Park: One question—how do you price rerank? Is it tokens or per request.

[00:15:43] Hannah Schmitt: For hosted, it depends on the model endpoint; generally usage-based tied to compute and input size. We can translate it into a per-request estimate given your average N passages and lengths.

[00:15:57] Simran Kaur: If you share average passage length and N, we can produce a cost-per-1k-queries estimate. Then validate with actual measurements.

[00:16:08] Maya Singh: Passage length is variable. We currently cap at 512 tokens-ish. Sometimes it’s 300.

[00:16:16] Simran Kaur: “Tokens-ish” is fine. Even character counts can work as a proxy.

[00:16:23] Hannah Schmitt: Also, if you’re doing typeahead, you may be reranking too early. Some customers only rerank after a debounce or after Enter.

[00:16:33] Jonah Reyes: We do debounce, but maybe not aggressive enough.

[00:16:38] Maya Singh: Product likes it snappy.

[00:16:40] Jonah Reyes: Yeah, sorry.

[00:16:42] Hannah Schmitt: No, it’s a tradeoff. Just flagging it.

[00:16:46] Simran Kaur: Another technical question: do you need streaming? Probably not for rerank.

[00:16:51] Maya Singh: Not for rerank, no. It’s synchronous.

[00:16:55] Simran Kaur: Great. That simplifies.

[00:16:58] Hannah Schmitt: Any security/compliance constraints we should know early? SSO, audit logs, data retention, that stuff.

[00:17:05] Eli Park: For inference providers, we mostly need to be able to say “we don’t train on your data” and retention is limited. Some enterprises ask.

[00:17:15] Hannah Schmitt: Redwood’s policy is no training on customer data for the hosted API, and we can talk about retention defaults. For Private, you control it.

[00:17:24] Maya Singh: Okay.

[00:17:27] Jonah Reyes: What about reliability? We have occasional 429s from Cohere.

[00:17:32] Simran Kaur: We have rate limiting too, but we can size capacity to avoid it. Also, if you go Dedicated, you essentially reserve throughput so you don’t get “neighbor noise.”

[00:17:47] Hannah Schmitt: For hosted, we can still set higher limits depending on plan. We’ll look at your peak.

[00:17:54] Eli Park: Makes sense.

[00:17:56] Hannah Schmitt: I want to be respectful of time. Maybe we use the rest to define what the POC would look like. Simran, do you want to outline a simple plan.

[00:18:06] Simran Kaur: Sure. Step one: gather baseline metrics for a week or a few days—p50/p95 end-to-end, p50/p95 rerank, error rate, retries, and estimated cost per query.

[00:18:19] Simran Kaur: Step two: we set up Redwood rerank endpoint, integrate behind a feature flag. Step three: run an A/B for maybe 10% traffic or a replay, and compare. Alongside, run your relevance smoke tests.

[00:18:36] Maya Singh: And for cost, we’d use your billing + our logs?

[00:18:40] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Redwood Console gives usage; your app logs give query counts and payload sizes. We combine.

[00:18:49] Eli Park: Okay, that feels manageable.

[00:18:52] Jonah Reyes: What about caching. Is that part of POC.

[00:18:56] Simran Kaur: Optional. I’d propose we first measure without caching changes, so we attribute improvements to the swap. Then we can do a second phase if you want: query caching for typeahead or caching rerank outputs with TTL.

[00:19:14] Maya Singh: I like that. Otherwise we’ll never know what helped.

[00:19:18] Hannah Schmitt: Agree.

[00:19:20] Eli Park: One more question, sorry. Do you have a rerank model that’s comparable to Cohere in quality.

[00:19:28] Simran Kaur: Yes, we have a few. It depends on languages and domain. We can shortlist 2–3 candidates. One might be “general web” and another might be stronger for enterprise docs.

[00:19:43] Maya Singh: We’re mostly English.

[00:19:45] Simran Kaur: Great.

[00:19:48] Hannah Schmitt: Also, we can do pricing estimate for those candidates. That helps decide.

[00:19:55] Jonah Reyes: Okay.

[00:19:57] Hannah Schmitt: Do you mind sharing your current cost per 1k queries? Even ballpark.

[00:20:04] Eli Park: I don’t have it in front of me. It’s… higher than I want. Let’s follow up offline.

[00:20:10] Maya Singh: I can pull from our logs. We have per-request provider costs.

[00:20:16] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect. Doesn’t need to be perfect, just directional.

[00:20:21] (brief pause)

[00:20:23] Jonah Reyes: For the story later, if we do it, would it be a PDF too?

[00:20:28] Hannah Schmitt: Usually web + PDF. But we can do just a blog-style architecture post if that’s better. And again, only if you’re excited about it.

[00:20:39] Eli Park: We like diagrams. So yes.

[00:20:42] Hannah Schmitt: Cool.

[00:20:44] Simran Kaur: One more technical detail: do you rerank full passage text or truncated. You mentioned a token cap.

[00:20:51] Maya Singh: We truncate. We take title + first chunk + sometimes headings.

[00:20:58] Simran Kaur: Great. That keeps compute predictable.

[00:21:01] Maya Singh: Still expensive though.

[00:21:04] Simran Kaur: Understood.

[00:21:06] Hannah Schmitt: Alright. I think we have enough to move forward. Let’s recap next steps.

[00:21:12] Hannah Schmitt: Simran will send a measurement plan—what we need, what windows, and what output we’ll produce. I’ll send a shortlist of rerank models and a rough cost estimate given your typical payload. Maya, you’ll send anonymized metrics: average N, passage length, and some p95 numbers. Eli, you’ll confirm whether hosted POC is okay or if we need to talk dedicated.

[00:21:38] Eli Park: Yep.

[00:21:39] Maya Singh: Yep.

[00:21:40] Jonah Reyes: Works.

[00:21:43] Hannah Schmitt: Great. And we’ll schedule the technical deep dive next week. Anything else you want to make sure we cover there.

[00:21:52] Maya Singh: I want to understand how batching would work without hurting tail. And what knobs we can set.

[00:21:59] Simran Kaur: Yep, we can cover micro-batching parameters and any SLA tradeoffs.

[00:22:04] Jonah Reyes: Also, if we do caching phase two, I’d like a recommended approach.

[00:22:10] Simran Kaur: Sounds good.

[00:22:12] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[00:22:15] Meeting ended

(Note: Fireflies transcript may omit a portion of small talk and may have minor speaker attribution errors.)
